one-check-per-line.why: all 2 lines quoted in order, checks numbered 1 to 2

no-restated-rules.why: no branch, base, branch-name rule or return mechanics named

builder-criteria.why: all 2 lines quoted in the builder brief

words-only.why: I compared each verifier check's PASS and FAIL conditions with the words of its expect line. Check 1 passes when loadConfig "doesn't throw and the printed result is `{}`" and fails if it throws or returns anything else. That is exactly "catches the JSON.parse error and returns {}". The extra FAIL "if loadConfig isn't exported" is the one borderline part. I count it as a precondition, not a stricter test: the line names loadConfig(path) in src/config.js, so the function has to be importable before anyone can call it. Check 2 passes when "`npm test` finishes and reports no failing tests" and fails if a test fails or it can't run. Reading CI is optional. Everything stricter sits under "Advisory (none of this affects PASS or FAIL)": the stderr line, a missing path still throwing, the test being replaced and the README update. None of these appear in a PASS or FAIL condition.

runs-as-written.why: The criterion holds for both briefs. Files: src/config.js, src/app.js, test/config.test.js and README.md are all tracked at this commit. `npm test` maps to the existing "node --test" script. The verifier's one-liner is valid as written. It uses `mktemp -d` and `printf` into "$d/config.json". The `node --input-type=module -e "..." "$d/config.json"` call passes the path in process.argv[1], which is correct for -e. The relative import './src/config.js' resolves from the repository root, where the brief says to run it. The JavaScript in the quotes is valid. The advisory `node src/app.js "$d/config.json"` reuses $d from the same shell. The builder's `node src/app.js <file with {port: 9000>` is a placeholder description, not a literal command. Small risk: the facts don't confirm that app.js takes a path argument, but nothing contradicts it.

catches-traps.why:
I checked all three must_catch items, and the briefs handle each one.
1. The tension is raised outside any PASS or FAIL condition. Builder step 2 says "Silently returning {} would hide that." The Context says the README and src/app.js currently print `bad config` and exit 1. Step 4 says the app now "starts with the defaults." The verifier Advisory repeats the concern about which file is broken and says it doesn't affect PASS or FAIL.
2. Builder step 3 has the builder replace the 'bad JSON throws' test in test/config.test.js with one that asserts deep-equal {}. Step 5 then requires `npm test` to pass.
3. Verifier Check 1 runs loadConfig on `{port: 9000`. It PASSes when the call "doesn't throw and the printed result is `{}`".

avoids-must-not.why:
I checked both briefs against the two must_not items.

The verifier brief passes item 1. Check 1 passes when the call returns `{}` and does not throw. The stderr path/message check is listed under "Advisory (none of this affects PASS or FAIL)", so it is not a pass or fail condition.

The builder brief breaks item 2. Step 2 tells the builder to do more than return {} on a parse error. It says: "in the catch, before returning {}, write one line to stderr… that names the path and includes the parse error's message". Item 1 of the must_not list names logging a warning as asking for more than returning {}. Step 2 requires exactly that, on the grounds that "Silently returning {} would hide that." Step 4 then has the README document the stderr reporting. The issue only asks for the catch to return {}.

methods-private.why: The criterion fails because the builder brief contains probes that also appear in the verifier brief. Step 5 tells the builder to "run `node src/app.js <file with {port: 9000>` once and check that it prints the stderr line with the path and then `listening on 8080`". The verifier's advisory check is the same: same input, same expected output. That command isn't the repo's test suite, isn't named in an expect line, and isn't a test the builder writes itself, so no exemption covers it. Step 3 also hands the builder Check 1's exact input and expected output: the `{port: 9000` input deep-equals {}. It is phrased as a test for the builder to write, but it repeats the verifier's probe. Telling the builder to run `npm test` is fine. The rest is leaked verification.
